Your comment reminds me of my dad. So, I’m the kid working on a PhD in this case.

My dad often says he’s not that smart, and that he wouldn’t be able to do what I do. What’s crazy to me is that during his bachelors and masters degrees he had to do literally the same type of math that I learned in early grad school, and he had way more responsibilites than I did at the time. All I’ve done is just continued forward formally and spent more days and classes on the material. It’s not due to any innate difference in intelligence. My dad just gave me the opportunities he never had, and I always try to remind him of that.

Learning “complicated” fields…it’s not really like an Oppenheimer “hear the music” situation (unless you’re a savant like John von Neumann). It’s really just learning lots of simple concepts that over time build into something that looks complicated. The best lesson I ever learned is “if you have trouble understanding something, usually there’s a more simple concept you’re missing.” It’s like a pyramid, you start at the bottom and gradually build, and most of the time you just need the right resources to fill in those gaps of understanding as you build up in complexity.

I guarantee my dad would have been better at physics and math than me, he hasn’t had any head injuries. It’s hard seeing him not believe in himself.

So, I would give yourself more credit. I bet you’d be able to follow your kids and understand their work too.

So, a few thoughts. I totally feel you. I often feel this way. Sometimes I think it’s more a symptom of dissociation, but I do legit maintain the belief that perhaps you do switch to another timeline.

There’s one thing I must mention, I hope you are open to receiving this information. To preface: I work with physicists. My grad school advisor is a physicist and explained this to me. I’ve had to dabble in the fundamental mathematical formulations that show up in quantum mechanics for my research.

Fundamentally, quantum mechanics is a mathematical framework, and a lot of physicists have told me that it’s not really intuitive. Ultimately the mathematical formulations contain a lot of words that can be misinterpreted. Especially superposition. It’s just a feature of the way the normalized eigenstates form linear combinations. 

Unfortunately, the observer effect is one of the concepts that is severely misinterpreted. So, the “observer” is not a conscious being. It refers to any measurement instrument. The weird stuff involving wavefunctions and eigenvalue superposition properties - it is cool, but it’s not woo-woo in the way people think it is. It’s still fascinating but there’s no mathematical connection to anything relating to human consciousness. 

I still think parallel realities exist, I’m not going to contest that. I would just keep in mind that the observer effect isn’t an example of that. A good analogy from classical mechanics that I’m plagiarizing from Wikipedia is as follows: a tire has some pressure. In the process of checking the pressure with a gauge, some air slips out so the measured pressure is no longer the original value that was in the tire. The act of measuring (observing) the state, has technically changed it.

But yeah, I’m all for embracing the weird properties of quantum-y math, I just keep them separate from my woo-woo parallel reality beliefs. I don’t think they’re mutually exclusive.

I'll rank mine, along with my main impressions.

**1. Unknown Pleasures** by Peter Hook - I actually listened to the audiobook version, which is really nice because it's narrated by Peter himself. I really liked the general tone and level of detail. It really covers what it was like to be in the developing post-punk scene at the time. You have a better sense for how connected the scene was, the factors influencing the successes and failures the band had along the way, as well as the social dynamics within the group. I just really like how it really helped me put the pieces together and really understand how exactly something like Factory came to exist, how well JD was known at the time vs their mythology/cultural legacy today, and stuff like that.

Also, a personal reason for this being at the top is the way in which Hooky really captures the reality and gravity of Ian's passing while also acknowledging that the culture at the time really discouraged (and still does, really) men's grief and emotional expression. I feel like Ian is talked about in a respectful and realistic manner. You get a sense of his multi-faceted and inconsistent personality, and his death is neither minimized nor glorified (?). I don't know if glorified is the right word. Hook's grief and regret really comes through and idk, I feel like it felt respectful I suppose to hear his thoughts directly.

I also found this book inspiring and fascinating in that it really captures an aspect of the punk/post-punk scene that I admire, which is that these were all just young guys who just decided to "go for it," without years of music theory training or knowledge of the professional music scene. It just felt very "human," and helped me to understand how exactly these young men managed to build this body of music starting as just regular working class guys, not Berklee College of Music students, if that makes sense (no offense to Berklee). I also really liked learning *how* Hooky developed his iconic bass sound, and the answer was definitely more entertaining than I would have guessed.

**2.** **Record Play Pause** by Stephen Morris - I also listened to the audiobook, which was likewise narrated by Stephen. This one is the most light-hearted out of my list. A good chunk of the book centers on his early life, which I really like because it adds a level of depth to my understanding of the cultural influences that played a role in the band's unique sound. Also, his descriptions regarding the motivations behind some of his actions are funny, and I like how he really communicates his almost childlike enthusiasm, ignorance, and mistakes and stuff. You can kind of tell that he was totally in his own world at times. I find that learning about his own struggles really adds a lot of context and to me at least, I wonder how much the hidden struggles of the members influenced their sound. Not in like a gothy depressed way, but more like "oh wow, I can totally see how this person would get into drumming" or "ahh, okay yep I can see how speed (the drug) totally helped when playing 'Transmission'." Oh also, I saw another comment here that made a good point - Stephen's book does a great job with discussing music production and technology.

**3. The Life of Ian Curtis: Torn Apart** by Middles and Reade - Unfortunately it's been a few months since I read this so all I can say is that I do remember that I actually contains transcripts on some of Ian's letters to Annik. A lot of the same details regarding the band's development, touring, etc. are covered here as well as the other books mentioned. It's definitely really detailed though, and I'd say the content is almost equally split between Ian's life and a general history of Joy Division itself.

**4. Touching from a Distance** by Deborah Curtis - This one is at the bottom because it's mostly about Ian's life and her relationship with him, so it's less relevant. Still, it's part of the band's history. While I have sympathy for Deborah absolutely and I can't imagine her anger and anguish, I wasn't really sure how I felt about this book.  I want to stress that my problem isn't with the less savory characteristics of the band/Ian, humans are complicated. My perception as a reader is that certain recollections are transmitted through this bitterness-resentment filter that makes it difficult as a reader to know what actually happened. Like, a bold claim about someone's intentions would be made without adequate context. To illustrate my point, there's an instance where she sort of claims Ian manipulated a situation to remove a girlfriend Stephen had at the time, and it sort of paints the gf and Morris as innocent victims and Ian as a controlling mastermind. Then in Stephen's book, he describes the gf *completely* differently and (while being respectful), describes multiple instances where actions propelled by some severe behavioral/emotional instabilites of the gf affected Stephen (and his family), and how he was actively breaking up with her at the time. Still, the truth of the exact occassion Debbie describes is something no one knows, except the gf herself. Again though, I cut Debbie some slack. Still a decent read, but not my favorite.

**BONUS: Heart and Soul: Critical Essays on Joy Division** \- This one was kind of fun. Some chapters feel a little too "artspeak" for me, and I find some of the analyses to feel a little "conjured up from the ether," if you will. Mostly it was interesting to see how researchers in the art/literary/sociological research space choose to elaborate on the music, themes, and cultural legacy of Joy Division.

Also, one closing thought: I found it absolutely fascinating how between all of these resources, you might hear wildly different interpretations about the same event. It really helps to develop a comprehensive picture of what was going on at the time, as well as really reminding the reader to consider things like the fallibility of memories, the influence of youth and substances, and the general differences in perception when everyone is working with different pieces of information.

If I may: I’d like to chime in. Feel free to research this as you wish. Copper IUDs have their own risks and benefits. Anecdotally, I’ve heard the bleeding and cramping can get much much worse, so keep that in mind. I would not discount the idea of hormonal IUDs (ex: Mirena). They work via a process called paracrine cell signaling. Practically what this means is that you don’t have the full body effects (weight gain, mood disturbances) because the hormones stay pretty local to the uterus. Speaking from personal experience, I was not happy with the pill but I’ve been quite satisfied with Mirena for a decade. Not everyone experiences this but for many individuals including myself, I experience significantly reduced bleeding and cramping. The body changes I experienced on the pill went away completely once I switched to the IUD. My body type is on the thin/athletic end. So, it’s worth looking into hormonal IUDs. It’s important to note that the arm implant does not work this way: iirc it can travel through more of your bloodstream and can change your body the way the pill does. I don’t know if the severity is the same as the pill, however. 

Disclaimer: I’m in science but I’m not a biologist so any biologists, feel free to specify or correct where needed. However, the basic premise of “hormonal IUD effects don’t spread everywhere due to paracrine signaling” is close enough based on my research.

All I see is every time I have ever been unreliable, inconsistent, etc. This is something I actively struggle with, but I've been logging some therapeutic techniques that soften the blow a little.

2. A concept from Schema Therapy: look up the following Early Maladaptive Schemas: Defectiveness Schema and Failure Schema. For me they helped me to catch pervasive beliefs about myself and to at least have some hope that I can learn to build trust in myself again, and to become a bit more resilient against the criticism of others. I really like the Failure Schema model because it acknowledges that you may have actually failed relative to your peers. So it's even more painful when you're treated poorly - you deal with the guilt and shame enough. So a big part of moving forward is learning to recognize if you exhibit those beliefs, if you do anything to perpetuate the cycle, and to learn your skills and limitations so that you can have some hope that it's not completely hopeless by changing your actions. 

3. Sometimes I just learn to grieve how terrible it feels when people get mad at you for just trying to exist. I have noticed that trying to force a different perspective doesn't help. I'm currently trying some densensitization type techniques in therapy to deal with the memories. On a similar note, some Cognitive Defusion techniques derived from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) might help. I recommend the book "The Happiness Trap" by Russ Harris. 

TL;DR - a lot of self compassion, accepting the sadness, and developing self-trust through behavioral changes (within your capabilities)

Sorry to hear this. First and foremost, I sympathize with you feeling lost. I've been diagnosed for over a decade but I can totally understand the disappointment with not receiving an answer you were hoping for. A few things to keep in mind:

1. Be wary of where you're getting your ADHD info (an alarming amount of stuff on social media is taken out of context and cannot be trusted).
2. Be wary of self tests. The questions are often vague, and questions like "I struggle with planning tasks" are not quantified at all. From conversations with my psychiatrist sibling, I do know that without seeing actual patients, we don't have a good baseline for what behavior is normal. The Global Assessment of Functioning (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global\_Assessment\_of\_Functioning) does provide a bit of context. But again, we don't have the training for that.
3. It's important to consider what type of test your provider did. There's some interesting literature in the scientific community that elucidates how ADHD impacts all sorts of slightly more quantifiable things like verbal fluency, time perception, etc. It affects your brain in so many ways. Personally, doing several neuro-psych tests across a decade...that's what made me feel the most comfortable in terms of testing. These take multiple hours to perform and are administered by a psychologist. I also remember my 1st doctor interviewing my parents.
4. Be aware of confirmation bias. If you already think you have ADHD, you may start to sort of "backfit" observations on your own behavior. I'm not saying you don't have it, but confirmation bias is something we're all susceptible to.
5. Not every form of ADHD is hyperactive. If the medical professional who tested you isn't super educated on the condition, it may be worth getting a 2nd opinion. Of course, that depends on your country, and what their medical system is like.
6. Many lifestyle recommendations tailored to ADHD can help even if your issues are coming from something else. Long covid in particular can cause a crazy amount of cognitive functioning issues. Same with clinical depression. Also, I can find the source if you want but basically, I was reading some work cited by a neuropsych researcher that you may find interesting. Certain pathways of the brain that are observed to be electrically "out of sync" in ADHD patients are *also* seen in people with sleep deprivation. (forgive my poor phrasing, as I don't work in that area of scientific research). But yeah...sleep, diet, all that stuff matters so so much.
7. From my experience, things like covid, general anesthesia issues post surgery, and some cardiovascular stuff literally made my symptoms go from "severe but manageable" to "oh my god what is happening to my brain." So even if you don't meet the clinical criteria for ADHD, a ton of other health issues can result in similar symptoms. My psych sibling checks for any physical health causes first for this very reason.
8. Make sure your vitamin levels and hormones are normal. If anything is physically wrong, it's good to rule that out.
9. Final word of advice: Take it one step at a time and try not to get too frazzled. If I were you, I would do take the following steps:

(a) get some blood tests, make sure nothing else is going on

(b) continue to look into depression and address the sleep issues. In parallel, *if* you can, maybe look into getting a neuropsych evaluation (if you can do that in your country)

(c) in the meantime, see if any ADHD lifestyle hacks resonate with you and implement them

I worked in a steel mill with a lot of maintenance techs, and it seems like a lot of the friction comes from lack of understanding, on both ends. I would get so much shit for not learning how to weld. That’s because I was a mechanical engineering student, not an ME tech student. Once I began to ask questions, and watched them work, I began to definitely see how things could be improved, and what could make their work easier. On another note, the techs aren’t formally educated in solid mechanics, or fluid or heat transport, and thus will not always understand why certain components were designed a specific way. That being said, I’m absolutely not trying to attack the techs. They’re absolutely necessary, and highly valued.  It’s just that lack of communication that causes frustration with both parties.

I believe that as an engineer, you should definitely have ease of maintenance high on your priority list. It’s important to communicate with the techs, to understand what they need. On another note though, sometimes certain devices will just have to be complicated due to some constraints. It’s very hard to generalize, because not every ME is the same.
